topic.subject: science
topic.title: Force and pressure
topic.scope: force as push or pull, contact and non-contact forces, effects of force, pressure and area, liquid and atmospheric pressure

misconceptions.statement: An object in motion must have a force constantly acting on it.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the state of motion with the cause of motion based on everyday experiences like pushing a cart.
misconceptions.fix: A force is only needed to change the state of motion of an object, not to maintain a constant speed.

probe.question: If you stop pushing a moving toy car, why does it stop?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the force pushing it is gone, so it cannot move anymore.

misconceptions.statement: Forces only exist when there is visible movement.
misconceptions.why: Students equate force with visible physical work or displacement.
misconceptions.fix: Forces can act on objects without causing motion, such as when you push a heavy wall that does not move.

probe.question: Is there a force acting on a book resting on a table?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the book is not moving.

misconceptions.statement: Gravity is a force that only acts on objects falling downwards.
misconceptions.why: Students associate gravity only with the act of falling rather than a constant pull towards the Earth's center.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity is a non-contact force that acts on all objects at all times, pulling them towards the center of the Earth.

probe.question: Does gravity act on a ball while it is moving upwards?
probe.wrong_answer: No, gravity only pulls it down once it starts falling.

misconceptions.statement: Pressure is the same as force.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language, the terms are often used interchangeably to describe how hard something is pushed.
misconceptions.fix: Pressure is defined as the force acting on a specific unit of surface area; it depends on both the force and the area.

probe.question: Why is it easier to cut vegetables with a sharp knife than a blunt one?
probe.wrong_answer: Because you apply more force with the sharp knife.

misconceptions.why: Students visualize air as a heavy blanket resting on top of things.
misconceptions.fix: Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions because air molecules move randomly and collide with surfaces from all sides.

probe.question: Does the air exert pressure on the underside of a table?
probe.wrong_answer: No, air pressure only pushes down on the top surface.
